title: The empires' stories
summary: Every empire gained its own story, its own look and its own people. Athens, Sparta, Mycenae, Ionia and the Cyclades each have a main quest drawn from their myths and history and told in the old poets' manner, over three hours with the Minoan story. The quests now keep ships and items waiting in other systems until you arrive. Kilon Alios stands on every world as the narrator of New Hellas, and all 303 lines are voiced. Each empire has its own procedurally drawn buildings, furniture and dinosaur citizens. Saves load behind a loading screen, gear comes off the automaton with a click or a drag, every page fits at 150% text with nothing under 12 px, Esc closes windows, icons carry labels, and wrecks show on the minimap. Everything still runs at 240 FPS or more.

steps.title: Five empires, five stories
steps.text: Every empire now has its own main quest, starting at its capital: Athens' withering olive, Sparta's betrayed gates, the stolen gold mask of Mycenae, the eclipse foretold in Ionia and the drifting isle of Delos. Each one follows its people's own myths and history, with gods, oracles and the game's own monsters as bosses, told the way the old poets told their stories. Together with the Minoan story they take over three hours.

steps.title: Quests that never strand
steps.text: A quest that sends you to another system now waits for you: its ships and items are kept as records and appear when you arrive. Ships still alive when you jump away are there when you come back, and each ship is tagged so its loss counts. Markers attach to the system that holds their place. Old saves gain the new stories automatically.

steps.title: Kilon Alios, the narrator
steps.text: Kilon Alios now stands on every world and talks with you. Ask him who he is, who you are, what your mission is and what you might become. Away from home he tells the history, gods and great deeds of the people who hold that world, and the story of all New Hellas: how it began, who built the gates and why the empires quarrel. He narrates every empire's quest.

steps.title: Each empire's own buildings
steps.text: Buildings on an empire's worlds are no longer recoloured Minoan art. Each empire has its own walls, floors, roofs, columns, roof crowns and decorations, drawn by a procedural generator from a short spec of its colours, stonework and motifs. Edit the spec and run the generator again to redesign them.

steps.title: Their people and their furniture
steps.text: On an empire's worlds every citizen is one of its people, with its own dinosaur head, colours and names: Spartan tyrannosaurs with horsehair crests, Athenian raptors, Mycenaean dome-heads, Ionian crested duckbills and Islander spinosaurs. Their rooms are furnished in their own forms, 44 pieces per empire, from Spartan reed beds to Ionian star-map rugs.

steps.title: Voices for every line
steps.text: All the new dialogue is spoken: 303 lines, three times as many as before. Every Greek name was checked against how the voice actually reads it, and eleven that came out wrong were fixed. The voice tool now remembers what each recording says, so changing how a name is spoken records its lines again.

steps.title: Loading, saves and wrecks
steps.text: Loading a save now shows a loading screen that names the slot and what is being restored, with a bar that follows the planet as it is built. Loading a save no longer leaves a trader stuck at a destroyed station, which had stopped trade across the galaxy. Wrecks waiting to be salvaged appear on the minimap as grey diamonds.

steps.title: Taking gear off the automaton
steps.text: Gear comes off the automaton with a click on its slot or by dragging it back to your items, as well as with a right-click. Equipping or taking something off no longer makes the panel jump, and its text keeps your chosen size after the change.

steps.title: Screens that fit at any text size
steps.text: Every station, Ship Computer, Field Computer and settings page now fits without scrolling at 130% and 150% text, with columns sharing the page instead of leaving it half empty. No text in the game is smaller than 12 px, and anything built later, such as a row added or a panel refreshed, takes its screen's text size automatically.

steps.title: Esc, labels and the quest sign
steps.text: Esc now closes whatever window is open before it opens the Esc menu, and in Talos it leaves to the title screen. Exit works again after visiting the Library or Versions. Every icon button shows a short name beside its icon. The quest sign is a hollow yellow targeting triangle.

steps.title: Ephestos and New Hellas
steps.text: The smith-god who made you is called Ephestos throughout. The whole galaxy of 58 systems is New Hellas, and the Atrapos sector is the region around Knossos where you start. The welcome line names the system you are in. The infographics in Versions use bigger text and are checked automatically, so their labels stay inside their boxes and never overlap.

review.intro: Patch 0012 in code: five empire main quests written as data by a generator (tools/empire_quests.py -> data/scenarios.json), a scenario engine that keeps ships, items and markers waiting in other systems (scenarios.gd, scenario_host.gd), Kilon Alios's conversation and narration on every world (quest_data.gd, planet_surface.gd), each empire's procedurally drawn buildings, furniture and citizens (tools/empire_tiles.py, empire_furniture.py, empire_citizens.py; minoan_tiles.gd, furniture.gd, surface_props.gd), the loading screen (load_veil.gd), the GUI fitting any text size with a 12 px floor (ui.gd, settings.gd and the pages), Esc and icon labels everywhere, readable patch diagrams (patcher.gd), and fixes to trade after loading (galaxy.gd). Tests: test_empire_quests, test_text_sizes, and new checks in test_saves, test_menus_fit, test_frontier and test_editor.

@@ -4,12 +4,12 @@ # basics | Getting started
 Your first steps, the controls, and how this guide and the game's tooltips work.
 
 ## start | Welcome, pilot | keywords: Respawn, Load saved game, Main menu, CRT filter, attract mode
-You fly a light fighter in the Atrapos sector, a galaxy of 58 star systems where six Greek star empires, the independents and the Sea Peoples raiders compete. Destroy raiders, collect what they drop, trade, take quests, and spend your credits on better ships, equipment and technology.
+You fly a light fighter in **New Hellas**, a galaxy of 58 star systems - you start in its Atrapos sector, round Knossos - where six Greek star empires, the independents and the Sea Peoples raiders compete. Destroy raiders, collect what they drop, trade, take quests, and spend your credits on better ships, equipment and technology.
 - **Click** empty space to fly there; **click an enemy** (red) to attack it; fly over glowing **loot** to collect it.
-- You start in orbit above **Amnissos** - its **land** button takes you down to walk around - near **Kephala Outpost**. Land on Amnissos first: **Kilon Alios**, the hooded wanderer by the landing pad, gives you the story. Click a station to dock: repair, trade, outfit, and pick up jobs (**Missions**). A glowing **yellow bulb** floats over whoever has a quest for you - Kilon until you take the story, stations while you have room for another mission.
-- **Tab** opens the [Ship Computer](doc:computer); **M** the sector map; **G** the galaxy map; **Esc** the menu (save, load, settings); **F1** this guide.
-- **Saving**: **Esc > Save Game** shows **6 save slots** - each with when it was saved, where you were (the system, and the planet if you were on one), your ship and credits. Pick an empty slot, or save over one (click it twice: it asks first). **Load** (in the menu or on the title screen) shows the same list; the delete button (twice) erases a save. A save made **on a planet** loads back **down there, where you stood**. **F5 quicksaves** (its own Quicksave slot) and **F9 quickloads** it - anywhere, in space or on a planet (rebind them in Settings > Controls). The game also **autosaves** (its own Autosave slot) - every 5 minutes at first, never while you're under attack - and whenever you dock, arrive in a new system or land: **Settings > Game** chooses how often (off, or every 2, 5, 10, 15 or 30 minutes) and whether docking, jumps and landings autosave too. Both show at the top of the Load list.
-If your ship is destroyed, **Respawn** puts you in a new ship at the nearest station with everything you've done kept - the story, your missions, reputation and credits - except your cargo, a tenth of your credits (the insurance) and **one thing you carried** - a random stack from your inventory or a piece of your toolbar's equipment (never the basic laser or a story item). @@ -68,6 +68,83 @@ # Spoken lines
 | kilon | bd525704755f88ac | 3.6 s | The signal will keep. So will I. Come back when you are ready. |
 | kilon | f03a2d30e29f7254 | 2.8 s | You still carry the thread. I can feel it pulling. |
 | kilon | a02976e433469b9e | 6.5 s | You followed it to the end, and they are remembered now - because of you. Thank you, pilot. |
+| kilon | a050e7af1dc06a69 | 4.1 s | Automaton. Ask, and I will answer what I can. |
+| kilon | a193aa36bc6d50d1 | 2.6 s | Go well, automaton. I will be here. |
+| kilon | addb09ffe3bc3708 | 5.9 s | I am Kilon Alios, the maintainer of this world. I keep its gears turning and its records true. |
+| kilon | 0b6f5f8112a26a8b | 9.5 s | I act under the commands of my god, Ephestos - lord of the forge, god of science and technology. His will is the hammer; I am the hand that holds it. |
+| kilon | 812259b9e0af3274 | 5.1 s | You are an automaton, built by Ephestos himself - no mortal smith's work. |
+| kilon | e878881d556615f9 | 6.5 s | He made you to improve, and to gather knowledge. Every world you walk and every voice you hear becomes a part of you. |
+| kilon | 711bb6f095695f5c | 8.5 s | Around us lies New Hellas: a collection of solar systems ruled by the great Hellenic empires, each with its own strengths and weaknesses. |
+| kilon | f19e34bc544e7628 | 9.7 s | The Minoans are the oldest and richest in learning, yet their worlds are short of bread. The Athenians trade, debate and sail the finest fleets - and quarrel among themselves. |
+| kilon | ee9c71cc9bf43283 | 8.1 s | The Spartans are all soldiers, few in words and unbending. The Mycenaeans are warrior-kings of gold and stone, proud and quick to feud. |
+| kilon | 0d17fa267758fee3 | 8.9 s | The Ionians measure the stars and would rather think than fight. The Cycladic Isles are old and calm, traders and sculptors, small among giants. |
+| kilon | de1c0bf6fb2265c5 | 7.0 s | Between them drift the Independents, who answer to no one - and beyond the charted lanes the Sea Peoples wait to prey on all of them. |
+| kilon | 9dd854f1c4bfb4bc | 6.6 s | To understand the world around you - and, through the cultures of these empires, to form your own opinion of who you are. |
+| kilon | a3466b623d014e73 | 5.5 s | And with what you become, you can help them prosper, and find a new purpose for their existence. |
+| kilon | 16a239c6d5279ba0 | 2.8 s | That is yours to decide. Your freedom is your own. |
+| kilon | e92fe3141b734f40 | 11.1 s | You may be a guardian, or a conqueror. An inspiration, or a dark mind acting behind the scenes. Or a free spirit, roaming the stars and acting only on your own will. |
+| kilon | 2ce602dff6245df9 | 10.1 s | Every empire has its own missions and goals - some good, some evil, some constructive, some destructive. You can tip the balance and shape their future, or choose not to be involved at all. |
+| kilon | 53619f332ec089af | 4.0 s | In the end, your only clear mission is this: to fathom your own potential. |
+| kilon | 8adb5b90283f6410 | 8.4 s | When the old sea grew too small for the children of Hellas, they built ships for the dark between the stars, as their fathers built ships for the wine-dark sea. |
+| kilon | dfaa9bc5dd0a5c2e | 14.0 s | Each people went out together and named their new worlds after the old: Athenai, Sparta, Mykenai, Miletos, Knossos, Delos. So the old land was carried into the sky, as a man carries fire in a pot. |
+| kilon | 56cf7a935db5cd9f | 6.1 s | They called the whole of it New Hellas: fifty-eight suns, six great peoples, and the free ports between. |
+| kilon | 30217519d16c2ba8 | 8.9 s | Ephestos, my maker, forged them at the bidding of Zeus - rings of bronze and fire at the edge of every sun, so that no people would be cut off from the others. |
+| kilon | 1a86cd5bb4bf0d42 | 8.7 s | The Cyclopes beat the metal; I was made to keep it bright. That is my work: I walk the worlds and see that the gates, and the people, hold together. |
+| kilon | 3693dfef15f3f2ad | 7.3 s | They pray to the same gods and sing the same songs, and so they quarrel - as brothers quarrel, more bitterly than strangers. |
+| kilon | 2713d68708a75b7a | 10.1 s | Athens loves its assembly, Sparta its discipline, Mykenai its gold, Ionia its questions, the Isles their quiet, the Minoans their memory. Each thinks its love the best. |
+| kilon | 8152cea252fb3817 | 5.4 s | And from beyond the charted lanes the Sea Peoples watch them quarrel, as wolves watch two bulls fight. |
+| kilon | ca27d0cefc1f8968 | 11.3 s | Near. They do not walk among men as they did in Homer's songs, but they speak - in the oracles, in a gate that flickers, in a monster that wakes when someone has grown too proud. |
+| kilon | d92fb15c6b5507e8 | 7.4 s | Honour the stranger, keep your oaths, give the gods their share and do not boast. That is all they have ever asked. It is harder than it sounds. |
+| kilon | 6234c4ac8d7d0749 | 8.6 s | The oldest corner of New Hellas, round Knossos, named for Atropos - the Fate who cuts the thread of life, and whom no god can overrule. |
+| kilon | a0ab5641131e22cb | 8.3 s | The Minoans keep secrets there older than the gates. Some say even older than me. The thread you follow begins there - and, I think, ends there too. |
+| kilon | 861d1d077104d6cd | 6.1 s | Welcome to the land of the Minoans, the oldest people of the sea. They were great before the others learned to sail. |
+| kilon | 9d7bf85d8532ab11 | 9.7 s | Long before Athens was a village, the Minoans ruled the sea from Knossos. Their ships went everywhere; their palaces had no walls, for the sea was their wall. |
+| kilon | 9200350c2ad3a6c5 | 6.9 s | They wrote in signs no one can now read, and painted their walls with dolphins, lilies and young people leaping over bulls. |
+| kilon | 0944af62dff86a7b | 8.4 s | A great goddess, who holds snakes in her raised hands, and the bull - Poseidon's beast. Their holy sign is the labrys, the double axe. |
+| kilon | 2a57aa221c791e3d | 9.0 s | In the Labyrinth beneath Knossos lived the Minotaur, son of a queen and a bull. Daidalos built the maze; Ariadne's thread led Theseus out of it. |
+| kilon | ddf7849146923ccc | 7.8 s | The island of Thera burst like a cracked pot, and the sea rose against Crete. After that the mainland kings came and took the palaces. |
+| kilon | 4cb362bb7934d1b1 | 4.7 s | But a people is not a palace. They remembered, and in New Hellas they rule again. |
+| kilon | b2fc1ca71c5a8688 | 6.7 s | You stand in the land of grey-eyed Athena. Here men argue in the assembly before they take up arms - and sometimes instead of it. |
+| kilon | 30861bf642691e98 | 7.4 s | A people of talkers, builders, sailors and thinkers. Every citizen may speak in their assembly, and every citizen does. |
+| kilon | 585b38b6d900321c | 8.3 s | Solon gave them laws, Kleisthenes gave them a voice, and Perikles built them the Parthenon. Then they quarrelled with Sparta, and lost much of it. |
+| kilon | 36cb14fa23a00727 | 9.4 s | Athena above all - wise in counsel and terrible in war, with her owl and her olive. Each year they carry a new robe to her in procession. |
+| kilon | 2bc66fabd15d89a1 | 6.1 s | Poseidon they honour too, carefully, for he lost the contest for their land and has never quite forgiven it. |
+| kilon | 9fdc420d0453765b | 8.3 s | At Marathon their hoplites ran at the Persians and broke them. At Salamis their ships, the 'wooden walls' of the oracle, broke the Persian fleet. |
+| kilon | 84cf906800bed7fd | 7.8 s | And in their theatres they invented tragedy and comedy - which may be the greater deed. Battles are forgotten; Sophokles is not. |
+| kilon | 705e2897a70e816a | 4.2 s | This is Lakedaimon. Speak briefly - they will like you better. |
+| kilon | a1e1e1f99220402c | 7.6 s | A people who made themselves an army. At seven their boys leave home for the agoge, the training, and they live by its rules until they are old. |
+| kilon | 7e1c7b132129fee0 | 7.8 s | Lykourgos gave them their laws and made their money of iron, so that no one could hoard it. They grew strong, and proud, and few. |
+| kilon | 263a15958550b092 | 9.3 s | Apollo of Amyklai, Artemis Orthia at whose altar boys showed they could bear pain, and Ares, whom they keep in chains in a temple so that war will never leave them. |
+| kilon | b5e6d3cf34abc152 | 8.8 s | And the Twin Stars - Kastor and Polydeukes, Spartan princes, sons of Zeus - who ride before their armies and save sailors in the storm. |
+| kilon | 4623fcb5a551664a | 11.8 s | Three hundred held the pass of Thermopylai against an empire, and died there to the last man but one. Their stone says: 'Go, tell the Spartans, passer-by, that here, obedient to their laws, we lie.' |
+| kilon | f736dcd1c74bfd38 | 6.3 s | Their kings claim descent from Herakles. Their women own land and speak their minds, which shocked the rest of Greece greatly. |
+| kilon | 54eb98ad3195f321 | 6.0 s | Mykenai, rich in gold. Look at the walls - no man built those. Or so they say. |
+| kilon | 77be49f0bb9fb733 | 7.9 s | The kings of the bronze age of the mainland, who went to Troy. They lived in citadels behind walls of giant stones and were buried with masks of gold. |
+| kilon | a24ad96939a38c11 | 5.4 s | Their king was the wanax, and every jar of oil in his storerooms was counted on clay tablets. |
+| kilon | 258077f76cbe104c | 7.6 s | Zeus and Hera, Poseidon, Hermes, Dionysos - their tablets name them, the oldest written names of our gods. |
+| kilon | a4f34cc925cf46a8 | 8.3 s | And the Cyclopes, one-eyed smiths, who forged Zeus's thunderbolts and, they say, lifted the stones of these walls. |
+| kilon | b0f2f7d6bbe18393 | 11.2 s | Agamemnon of Mykenai led a thousand ships to Troy. Perseus, who founded this city, killed the Gorgon; Herakles, born of its royal house, did his twelve labours for its king. |
+| kilon | e2c9f088c3f01c62 | 8.2 s | But their house was cursed. Atreus did a terrible thing, and each king after him paid for it. Pride, and the price of pride - that is their story. |
+| kilon | 4eaa7dc0e75bc6bc | 4.6 s | Ionia, where men first asked questions without waiting for the gods to answer. |
+| kilon | fd50a8b88bf46e26 | 8.4 s | Twelve cities on a bright coast - Miletos, Ephesos, Samos and the rest - rich with trade and full of restless minds. |
+| kilon | 6c6ebe3a72b4f25f | 8.3 s | Here Thales asked what the world is made of, Anaximander drew the first map, and Herakleitos said no one steps in the same river twice. |
+| kilon | 98af2581bb751283 | 10.5 s | Artemis of Ephesos, whose temple was a wonder of the world; Apollo at Didyma, whose oracle answered the Ionians; Hera on Samos, in the greatest temple of the Greeks. |
+| kilon | a4be9e972c45be98 | 7.0 s | And Poseidon at the Panionion, where the twelve cities met each year to sacrifice to him together - and to quarrel. |
+| kilon | ea9cae2ab7e95d65 | 7.6 s | They rose against the Persian king, and lost, and Miletos was burned. Yet the spark they lit became the war that freed Greece. |
+| kilon | 15551a2216e1d2ab | 9.7 s | And Homer, the singer of Troy and of Odysseus, was an Ionian, some say from Smyrna, some from Chios. Every Greek child learned to read from his songs. |
+| kilon | cd2ce4ec0cde0fc4 | 6.9 s | The Isles in their circle. The people here are old and quiet; they were carving marble when the rest of Greece was still learning to farm. |
+| kilon | 1cdc3399fdf47687 | 10.3 s | Sailors and traders of the Cyclades - the circling isles, set round holy Delos. Melos had its obsidian, Paros its marble, Siphnos its gold. |
+| kilon | 78ac31c68cc207f4 | 8.0 s | Their oldest makers carved white figures with folded arms and faces with only a nose. No one knows their names. Their work outlived every king. |
+| kilon | 44c96c4d04972786 | 9.8 s | Apollo and Artemis, born on Delos; Leto their mother, who found rest there. Dionysos, who found Ariadne weeping on Naxos and made her his bride. |
+| kilon | a71a2131d2727fa8 | 5.7 s | No one may be born or die on Delos; the island is the god's. Even the dead were moved away. |
+| kilon | 4ce278089353958c | 7.7 s | They do not boast of great deeds. They traded, they carved, they sailed. When Thera's mountain burst, they buried their town and lived on. |
+| kilon | 68b837371b065e28 | 3.7 s | Perhaps that is their great deed: they endured, when greater peoples did not. |
+| kilon | f0b404dc31a561ff | 4.1 s | A raiders' world. Keep your hand near your weapon and your purse closer. |
+| kilon | a9043a87b15624ff | 10.0 s | In the old days ships came from no one knows where - Shardana, Lukka, Danuna, Peleset - and burned the cities of the bronze age, from Ugarit to Pylos. |
+| kilon | 43eb7201a6cb9a62 | 8.5 s | The kingdoms fell and writing was forgotten for four hundred years. Their heirs in New Hellas raid the lanes, and the empires have not yet learned to stop them. |
+| kilon | 2ab1009728bc858a | 5.3 s | A free world. No empire holds it, and every empire trades here. |
+| kilon | 6e889302e11ecc44 | 9.8 s | Those who belong to no city: traders, exiles, ship-wrights, runaways. The old Greeks called such men metics - welcome, but never quite at home. |
+| kilon | 716d6131738ee4e6 | 5.8 s | Be kind to them. Zeus protects strangers, and you are a stranger too. |
 | kilon | 9b879541208df72f | 3.2 s | Where it leads now: Dock at Kephala Outpost. |
 | kilon | 52eccee134d2b4dc | 2.6 s | Where it leads now: Find the source of the signal. |
 | kilon | 0f0b59e3ff141fea | 3.3 s | Where it leads now: Destroy the raiders at the signal source. |

@@ -85,4 +162,148 @@ # Spoken lines
 | kilon | d2c22c0609e3ed51 | 2.3 s | Where it leads now: Enter the heart of the Labyrinth. |
 | kilon | 38802f343357b60d | 3.7 s | Where it leads now: Defeat the Minotaur, guardian of the Labyrinth. |
 | kilon | 64dfe4e702e3e6e2 | 2.1 s | Where it leads now: The thread is complete. |
+| kilon | 278820df0b969587 | 7.6 s | Sing, Muse, of the pilot who came to the city of grey-eyed Athena, when her olive withered and the sea rose against her people. |
+| kilon | 2f8c31554c9a685f | 12.5 s | Long ago, men say, two gods strove for the land: Poseidon struck the rock with his trident and a salt spring leapt out; Athena planted an olive. The people chose the olive, and the city took her name. |
+| daidalos | 73cd3433825bed0c | 7.0 s | Welcome, stranger. Sit, eat, and then tell me your name - so the custom of our fathers commands, and so I keep it. |
+| daidalos | 5c859bf372316588 | 10.2 s | Hear our grief. The olive in the garden-ring of the Akropolis, grown from the seed of the goddess's own tree, is withering. Salt is in its roots, and no engineer can say how it came there. |
+| daidalos | 9f6b5f6d2b59d20a | 9.8 s | When the wise do not know, the wise ask. Go to the silver mines of Laurion in the Marathon system. The priestess Diotima keeps the bronze owl there; it speaks with the voice of the goddess. |
+| kilon | dfcbe144c732cda3 | 8.2 s | Laurion: a grey moon riddled with old shafts, where the city's silver was dug by men who never saw the sun. There the owl keeps its watch. |
+| ariadne | e2a8a3b820214595 | 6.1 s | You come as the goddess said you would - unasked, and in a hurry. Sit. The owl does not speak to the hurried. |
+| kilon | d3c390407aac83a7 | 9.0 s | The sea's lord was robbed and has not forgotten. Where the cape of Sounion faces the dawn, thieves drank from his altar. Find them, and the salt will leave the root. |
+| ariadne | a8f9e4a8e7a64fac | 7.0 s | Sounion lies in the system of Athenai itself. The Sea Peoples have a den beyond our gates; it was they, surely. |
+| kilon | feaa78b6d668fcf0 | 7.7 s | At Sounion the raiders sat round their fires like wolves round a felled stag, and the bronze trident of Poseidon lay among them, black with soot. |
+| kilon | 4e41f45a0921c122 | 6.0 s | So the thieves fell, and the trident of the Earth-shaker lay in the pilot's hold - heavy as a guilty conscience. |
+| daidalos | f82c498aa65ac540 | 10.0 s | You have the god's trident? Then do not keep it an hour longer than you must. Gods are not asked twice. Bring gifts with it to the harbour-shrine at Piraeus: oil, wine and bread, as our fathers did. |
+| daidalos | cecb97dd2122eba2 | 4.8 s | Do not haggle over the gifts, pilot. A man who bargains with a god has already lost. |
+| kilon | 05f103843e97a8bc | 7.3 s | They poured the wine on the deck of the harbour-shrine and burned the bread, and the smoke went up to the dark between the stars. |
+| daidalos | c45fb1a11a3a5a8e | 7.2 s | The Earth-shaker has his trident and his gifts. Now set the trident back where it was taken, on the cape of Sounion, and say his name as you do it. |
+| kilon | 3a2c703b332bcead | 7.4 s | Then the pilot turned the ship back towards Sounion, carrying the god's own weapon through the god's own sea. |
+| kilon | dbf7757038f166e0 | 10.3 s | The trident was set in its place, and the pilot said the god's name. Far off, the gates of Athenai flickered once, as if a wave had passed through them, and were still. |
+| daidalos | 1e045ada72a24841 | 8.3 s | The salt is leaving the roots! But listen - the Sea Peoples have heard who robbed them of their prize. Their ships gather beyond Piraeus to burn our harbour. |
+| kilon | 2eef372cfc6ba95b | 6.8 s | In Piraeus the ships lay side by side like spears in a rack, and their crews sharpened their weapons and said little. |
+| daidalos | 877f61d34ede5d35 | 9.5 s | They are many and we are few. So we will not meet them in open space. We will meet them in the narrows before the gate to Ugarit, where their numbers are a burden and not a strength. |
+| daidalos | b8cc6f2e1847626d | 6.2 s | An oracle once told our fathers to trust in wooden walls. Our walls are hulls now. Yours is one of them. |
+| kilon | 8edd015f6850a92b | 7.2 s | As starlings wheel over a field before rain, so the raiders came through the gate, wheeling and crying on their radios. |
+| daidalos | 65fd48fd75e365e1 | 5.4 s | Their van is broken. But see - their great ships come behind, and their chief with them. Do not let them pass. |
+| radio | 9dfa79e8f79d909f | 4.0 s | Owl-folk! I will hang your ships from my mast like a fisher hangs his catch! |
+| kilon | eb0b310646418eaa | 6.9 s | So the chief fell in the narrows, and the sea of stars was strewn with wrecks as a beach is strewn with weed after a storm. |
+| daidalos | 3b2abefb6769ed7e | 8.2 s | Victory! Now the city must hear it before rumour reaches it first - rumour is quicker than any ship. Run, pilot, to the Stoa at Athenai, and do not stop. |
+| kilon | 047325f46eac1bc1 | 8.7 s | Once a runner ran from Marathon to the city with news of victory, spoke one word, and died. The pilot flew, and hoped for a kinder ending. |
+| daidalos | 78e92252f7513f3a | 4.3 s | Rejoice - we have won! You came faster than the rumour. The city will remember it. |
+| daidalos | 97ed5c922dc3d91e | 5.7 s | Rumour came before you, pilot, but it told the truth this once. No matter - you are here, and alive. |
+| kilon | cfd25595f2098385 | 7.5 s | That day the people walked in procession round the Akropolis-ring, as at the great festival, and carried a new robe to the goddess. |
+| daidalos | 8de063a9e6e81233 | 8.7 s | And look: the olive puts out new leaves. Grey-eyed Athena has seen it all. Take this, and take the city's thanks - you are a guest-friend of Athens, now and always. |
+| kilon | 06fc7329139c62a3 | 8.5 s | Sing, Muse, of Lakedaimon, the hollow land, whose people spend few words and many years of training - and of the stranger who stood among them. |
+| ariadne | 0fbc469172922f46 | 5.1 s | You. Pilot. We have a task. We do not give tasks to men we have not tested. |
+| ariadne | c7416a985d32b272 | 4.8 s | Raiders prowl the gate to Pylos. Three of them. Go alone. Come back. |
+| kilon | 7b59fe8c2338c8d8 | 6.7 s | When a king of Macedon wrote to them, 'If I enter your land I will destroy you,' the Spartans answered with one word: 'If.' |
+| kilon | 4351c9b3f3e5f9cb | 9.8 s | Spartan boys were sent out alone, with no shoes and one cloak, to live by their wits. The ephor asked the stranger for less than that - and watched closely all the same. |
+| ariadne | a943cacc0e279a95 | 0.7 s | Good. |
+| ariadne | 20bd83a960001dee | 7.2 s | Now the real task. Go to the shrine at Amyklai. The priest has an answer from Delphi. We do not like it. |
+| ariadne | 280b7114734283a6 | 6.3 s | Amyklai. The shrine of Apollo, where Hyakinthos died. Listen to the priest. Speak little. |
+| daidalos | 9dc9870c1cd225e9 | 7.2 s | Far-shooting Apollo gave this answer to our kings long ago, and gives it again: 'Love of money, and nothing else, will destroy Sparta.' |
+| daidalos | 56e72a4772c12119 | 12.4 s | Now hear what the god did not say, but we know. Leotychidas, once our polemarch, was sent into exile for taking a bribe. He has sold the codes of the Thermopylai gate to the Sea Peoples for a sleeve full of gold. |
+| daidalos | cd9d06b249c546d5 | 6.1 s | The garrison at Thermopylai Citadel must hold the pass. They are few. They are hungry. Bring them what they need. |
+| kilon | 0992c32f0434d853 | 9.2 s | Thermopylai: the hot gates. A narrow way between the mountains and the sea, where a few may hold back many - if they are fed, and armed, and do not run. |
+| daidalos | 0fc60e545279777f | 2.9 s | Bread and spears. Good. Now we can fight. |
+| daidalos | 68dd87bcec3ff933 | 6.9 s | A merchant told me their ships will be so many that their guns will hide the stars. Then we shall fight in the shade. Take your place at the gate to Lukka. |
+| kilon | d5f5e9571b3de06e | 5.7 s | They came through the narrow gate as a river comes through a gorge, and the Spartans stood in it like rocks. |
+| daidalos | 55ae703b19731948 | 3.3 s | First wave broken. They will send more. They always do. |
+| daidalos | 987617bd4f1fee71 | 4.6 s | There. The traitor's ship. He comes himself, to see what his gold has bought. |
+| radio | 455f2961ce10a5bf | 5.0 s | Spartans! I offer you what I was offered - gold, and your lives. Stand aside. |
+| kilon | b3f4bfb859d080fa | 5.3 s | The gold in his sleeve did not save him. It never does; that was the meaning of the god's answer. |
+| daidalos | 412b128bb21b8fed | 9.6 s | The pass holds. Now the Twin Stars. Kastor and Polydeukes, sons of Zeus, guard every sailor - their beacons at the Kastor Phalanx went dark when the raiders came. Relight them. |
+| kilon | 63b73273a690e386 | 7.6 s | Two stars, side by side, that sailors look for when the storm is worst. Their beacons had gone out the night the traitor's raiders came. |
+| kilon | a621c6ef7c3993d3 | 8.9 s | When the Twin Stars burn on a ship's mast, sailors say, the storm is over. The pilot set them burning again, and every ship in the lanes saw them. |
+| ariadne | 56aa53e29492c1b1 | 12.9 s | Bad news. At Tainaron, where the road to Hades opens, the three-headed hound has broken out. Herakles, father of our kings, dragged it up from below once. Now it is your turn. |
+| kilon | e64ed494eb9223f8 | 6.5 s | Three heads it had, and a mane of snakes, and its bark shook the hulls of ships as the bark of a dog shakes a sleeping house. |
+| kilon | c3ac3d519daa7670 | 5.2 s | So the hound of Hades went back down the road it came, and the gate of Tainaron was shut. |
+| ariadne | 1ea983772eea8274 | 2.4 s | Come back. Report. Keep it short. |
+| ariadne | 6fe85081b251f830 | 6.7 s | A Spartan mother tells her son, as she hands him his shield: 'With it, or on it.' You came back with yours. |
+| ariadne | 3f9ef4ea003dbc38 | 4.4 s | Take this. Few strangers are called friends of Lakedaimon. You are. |
+| kilon | 204720b69e0b4889 | 9.1 s | Sing, Muse, of Mykenai rich in gold, of its walls that the Cyclopes built, and of the curse that runs in its kings' blood like rust in a blade. |
+| daidalos | 30d0c2d61521d91f | 7.1 s | Stranger, you stand in the hall of the wanax. Drink from my cup - and then hear me, for the gods have turned their faces from my house. |
+| daidalos | 0a509b8f817776f2 | 6.9 s | The golden mask of my fathers was taken from the tholos-tomb, and the next night the Lion Gate's beacon went dark, and the great walls cracked. |
+| daidalos | d01e0c4fd60db20a | 7.8 s | Old Brontes, last of the Cyclops-engines, still tends the forge at Tiryns. He built these walls. Ask him what has broken them. |
+| kilon | 11d51870761b56ff | 7.4 s | Tiryns of the great walls: there the Cyclops-engine still beats its anvil, slow as a heart, as it has since the days of Perseus. |
+| asterion | e786675712fa346d | 9.7 s | One eye I have, and with it I have watched three thousand years. Walls do not crack by themselves, little one. A thief opened the tomb, and the dead were angry. |
+| asterion | 683e075142a47127 | 7.8 s | First mend the walls. Bring iron and titanium to the forge at the Lion Gate of Tirynthia, and I will set the stones as I set them for Perseus. |
+| asterion | 885e899cbf3e0705 | 5.4 s | Iron for the bones of the wall, titanium for its sinews. Bring them, and I will make it whole. |
+| kilon | 01ce88abdd6082f7 | 8.6 s | The forge roared like a lion in a cave, and the walls grew whole again, stone locked on stone, so close that no knife-blade could pass between them. |
+| asterion | 0079fcae0c37d817 | 6.5 s | The thieves took the mask towards the den of Lukka. Their sentries watch the gate from Mykenai. Clear the road. |
+| kilon | c9eb36edc9879026 | 5.1 s | The pass to Lukka: where the raiders watch, as crows watch a field from the top of a dead tree. |
+| daidalos | 111604a820e351f9 | 8.5 s | The road is open. But a worse thing stirs. In the marsh of Lerna, beside our own world, the many-headed serpent that Herakles killed has grown its heads again. |
+| daidalos | cc40322665d56d43 | 4.9 s | Herakles cut one head and two grew in its place. Do not be proud, pilot. Be patient. |
+| kilon | 533a19db3f83a1d9 | 4.8 s | Nine heads it had, and its breath was poison, and the marsh boiled where it moved. |
+| kilon | 3bc80c21b328de68 | 5.8 s | So the Hydra died a second time; and the pilot did not boast of it, remembering what happens to the proud. |
+| daidalos | e060539eaa0cc8d0 | 7.5 s | Now we sail to take back the mask. But the fleet cannot jump. The gates are still, as the winds were still at Aulis when Artemis was wronged. |
+| daidalos | d16bfb306fee2c5d | 6.3 s | Kalchas sees what was, what is and what will be. He has never told a king good news. Go and hear him anyway. |
+| daidalos | ef5c683517409627 | 7.2 s | Artemis is angry. One of the wanax's captains shot a hind in her sacred grove and boasted that not even the goddess could shoot better. |
+| daidalos | 888cc85a9e5a62d0 | 10.1 s | Once, at Aulis, she asked for a king's daughter. But in the better telling she took a hind instead, and carried the girl away to safety. Give her gifts of healing and clean water, and she will be content. |
+| daidalos | 4caaf928e47d7c3a | 6.7 s | Medicine for her healing hands, water for her clean springs. Artemis loves the wild things, and those who keep them whole. |
+| kilon | 65ea95a9b76cb62c | 8.4 s | They gave the goddess her gifts, and the captain who boasted gave her his bow. And the gates woke, one after another, like hounds hearing the horn. |
+| daidalos | 03c12e1982ef171a | 5.8 s | To Pylos! The thieves wait by the gate to Ugarit with the mask. Nestor's old city will see us pass. |
+| kilon | c38cf4470b440f4e | 8.4 s | Sandy Pylos, where old Nestor ruled - he who talked longest of all the Greeks at Troy, and was listened to, for he was wise. |
+| kilon | 3e9b3b3816f261b3 | 5.4 s | The thieves fell, and the golden mask lay in the wreckage, still smiling its calm gold smile. |
+| daidalos | eb42a4457fd0f092 | 10.0 s | Bring it home - but beware the sea between. Once Poseidon sent a monster, Cetus, against the land of Andromeda, until Perseus of our house killed it. My dreams say it is out again. |
+| kilon | 83c97cc7f278032f | 5.2 s | It rose from the dark as a whale rises from the deep, and its jaws could have swallowed a frigate whole. |
+| kilon | 8e1340f95d54877d | 2.9 s | So Cetus died, and the homecoming was free. |
+| kilon | 96a450ad49273a74 | 6.1 s | And so the pilot came home with the mask, as Agamemnon came home from Troy - but to a kinder welcome. |
+| daidalos | bc6eaef0a2c6e1e2 | 4.3 s | The mask is in the tomb again, and the Lion Gate burns. My fathers sleep. |
+| daidalos | 8a1d94b2f5846a0f | 11.2 s | Know this, guest: my house has a curse on it, from the day Atreus served his brother a terrible feast. Each king pays for the pride of the one before. You have bought us a little peace. Take gold for it - but take my friendship more. |
+| kilon | d6d4ad578cc79e50 | 6.7 s | Sing, Muse, of Ionia, where men first asked not which god made the world, but what the world is made of. |
+| daidalos | c97e9ef80a480969 | 7.8 s | Welcome, guest. I write down the stories of the Greeks - which are many, and, it seems to me, mostly foolish. Yours I would like to hear when it is finished. |
+| daidalos | 9be825c425d26cd6 | 9.2 s | Thales of our city foretold an eclipse of the sun, and it came on the day he named. Now the observatories say another is coming - one that will blind the gate-beacons of the whole League for an hour. |
+| daidalos | 49088f65212243b5 | 10.1 s | Worse: a raider named Herostratos boasts he will do a deed so great that men will speak his name for ever. Such men are dangerous. The League's council meets at the Panionion. Go and tell them. |
+| kilon | 652332cc9fc65d04 | 8.3 s | The Panionion stands on the headland of Mykale, where the twelve Ionian cities met each year to sacrifice to Poseidon and to quarrel. |
+| daidalos | 74e48eab7e91f28b | 10.1 s | Twelve cities sit in this council, and twelve cities never agree. But on this we agree: Ephesos must be guarded, and the eclipse must be measured, so that the gates can be steered by hand while it lasts. |
+| daidalos | 7ea6d9fc594260f7 | 7.5 s | Theano of Samos, who keeps the school of Pythagoras, is building the instrument. She needs parts. Bring them to the Sappho Observatory. |
+| ariadne | 880fa4e522353c53 | 11.3 s | Pythagoras taught that all things are number: the strings of the lyre, the rings of the planets, even justice. This instrument hears the numbers of the sky, and will tell us the second the shadow falls. |
+| ariadne | d5100e4dc96b9d29 | 6.2 s | Herostratos's scouts have been seen at Ephesos, by the strait. Drive them off before they learn too much. |
+| ariadne | 468f4cbbeadaeee7 | 4.9 s | Be quick and be careful. A man who wants to be remembered will do anything to be noticed. |
+| daidalos | a650b00593c563f9 | 11.1 s | The scouts carried fire-charges, the kind used to burn a station. Pilot - it is the temple of Artemis he means to burn. It is the greatest wonder of the League. Hurry to the temple-ring beside Ephesos Agora. |
+| kilon | af48b642952ec865 | 10.4 s | The temple of Artemis at Ephesos had a hundred and twenty-seven columns, each the gift of a king. Its ring now shone in the dark beside the Agora like a crown laid on black cloth. |
+| ariadne | b26123e42be44afa | 5.7 s | Too late to stop him reaching us - not too late to stop him finishing. He is here. Hear him. |
+| radio | f2932ac701ed3806 | 5.2 s | Let them burn my body afterwards! My name will outlive their temple, their League and their gods. |
+| radio | 660c49db111b730c | 4.8 s | Burn, ring of Artemis! Let the whole League see the fire, and say my name! |
+| kilon | a794b7a47cdd9a87 | 5.8 s | So Herostratos fell, and the temple stood, though its outer ring smoked for days. |
+| ariadne | 6ea9bb7745978ff3 | 9.7 s | The Ephesians have decreed that his name shall never be spoken or written again. That is the punishment the gods give the proud: what they wanted most, taken from them. |
+| daidalos | 6ae2cb4844647235 | 9.7 s | And yet I have just written it down. Well - a chronicler must. Now: the eclipse. Theano's instrument is at Miletos; be at the Pythagoras Artemision before the shadow falls. |
+| kilon | 241ef3543f40e328 | 6.3 s | The pilot flew towards Miletos, and behind the ship the light of the sun began, very slowly, to be eaten. |
+| ariadne | 60ff472e265083a1 | 7.0 s | In time! The numbers are true; the gates are steered. Thales would be proud - though he would pretend not to be. |
+| ariadne | 6cbdc896d0ce5582 | 7.4 s | The shadow came first - but the gates held, by luck and by the gods' patience. Next time, be quicker than luck. |
+| kilon | 39271c7ee43c3e0e | 9.2 s | And in the hour of the eclipse, when the stars came out at noon, something rose out of the strait of Lukka - six heads on long necks, and a girdle of barking dogs. |
+| daidalos | d142a3c9bb8c7a1e | 6.4 s | Skylla. Homer sang of her. Odysseus lost six men to her and could not fight her. You, at least, have guns. |
+| kilon | f26c6b7ba09da336 | 6.1 s | As a fisherman on a rock lets down his line and pulls up a fish, so she stooped from the dark and pulled ships from the lane. |
+| kilon | 1184df446989b195 | 5.6 s | So Skylla sank back into the strait, and the eclipse passed, and the sun came back to Ionia. |
+| daidalos | d41163b35e3a4df9 | 5.4 s | The singer at the Odeon has asked for you. Singers do not usually ask - they are usually asked. Go. |
+| daidalos | f23ede576b9fd5f7 | 9.8 s | Sit, guest. I am a singer, as my fathers were. I have made a new song - about a pilot, a burned temple that did not burn, and a monster that Odysseus could not kill. |
+| daidalos | 2986dfb012dd4e3d | 9.4 s | What is everything made of? Thales said water, Anaximenes air, Herakleitos fire, Pythagoras number. I say: stories. Take the League's gold - the song is free. |
+| kilon | 41274d3e734463e1 | 6.3 s | Sing, Muse, of the Isles that stand in a circle round holy Delos, as dancers stand round an altar. |
+| kilon | 8107bb96af1deaf1 | 18.0 s | Once Delos was a floating island, driven by every wind. When Leto, carrying the children of Zeus, wandered the world, no land would take her in - for they feared white-armed Hera. Only Delos dared. Then Poseidon fixed it to the sea's floor with four pillars, and there Apollo and Artemis were born. |
+| ariadne | 7d0ebfb2b473296f | 11.2 s | Guest, the Circle welcomes you - though you find us frightened. The four pillar-engines that anchor Delos are failing. The station has begun to drift, as the island drifted before the god was born. |
+| ariadne | 7685bac0f9944797 | 13.7 s | Each pillar was made with a gift from one isle: Siphnos gave gold, Melos obsidian, Paros marble, Naxos the vine. We must gather the gifts again. Begin with Siphnos - and remember what happened to the Siphnians who cheated the god. |
+| kilon | 733fe619f5ed9394 | 11.0 s | The Siphnians grew rich from their gold mines, and each year sent Apollo a golden egg. One year they sent gilded lead. The sea came into their mines, and they were rich no longer. |
+| daidalos | c1e14b4642075b87 | 8.5 s | A guest from the Circle! Sit; you shall have bread and figs before you have business. Then weigh your metal on our scales, and weigh it fairly. |
+| daidalos | b08e6b03d2fda224 | 5.5 s | True metal, honestly weighed. Our grandfathers should have done as much. The first pillar has its gift. |
+| daidalos | 7d83f40f4e4db88c | 6.8 s | Melos guards the black glass, obsidian - sharper than any bronze. But raiders have been robbing its quarries. Go carefully. |
+| kilon | dbb4f5175f80afae | 7.0 s | Melos: an island of black glass, whose people cut it into knives and arrow-heads long before the first smith blew on a fire. |
+| ariadne | 121758ecbed84b4a | 7.4 s | Our black glass is safe again. Take the best of it for the second pillar. Now Paros - the marble-cutters there are waiting for you. |
+| ariadne | 1045b52907953ac4 | 7.8 s | Paros. Its marble is so white that sculptors say it glows from inside. Ask for Arkesilas - he will complain, then help. |
+| daidalos | 546ed72389277861 | 8.3 s | You want marble for a pillar? Then you want white marble, the finest there is - not stone, light that has gone hard. But my cutters need metal for their saws. |
+| daidalos | 2c19405407df665a | 3.9 s | Bring metal. Not much - marble is patient, but my saws are not. |
+| daidalos | b324643e989a7d3e | 7.5 s | The third pillar has its marble. One isle is left: Naxos, where Dionysos found Ariadne weeping on the shore, and crowned her with stars. |
+| kilon | e2db181dea16dac6 | 11.9 s | Theseus left Ariadne asleep on Naxos and sailed for Athens. When she woke, his ship was a speck on the sea. But the god Dionysos came with his singing train, and made her his wife. |
+| ariadne | 178752c6b865f415 | 9.2 s | This is her crown - the one the god set in the sky as a ring of stars when she died. A copy, but a holy one. Take it to Delos; it is the fourth gift. |
+| ariadne | 53226d144e44bf8b | 7.6 s | But be warned. The white-armed queen of the gods has not forgotten Leto. She sent the serpent after her once. She has sent another. |
+| kilon | 19928953ebede296 | 9.4 s | Half a nymph she was, with lovely cheeks and bright eyes, and half a dreadful serpent - Echidna, mother of monsters, coiling round the drifting ring. |
+| ariadne | 96cae26d8a1e7cfd | 5.9 s | Leto's children were born on that rock against my will. Let the rock drift, and let it sink. |
+| ariadne | 732c8dae9eb84223 | 5.8 s | Do not answer her, pilot. One does not argue with the queen of the gods. One simply wins. |
+| kilon | 0a6b6f221eefd8ad | 6.8 s | So the serpent fell, as Python fell to Apollo's arrows; and the ring of Delos stood still on its pillars once more. |
+| kilon | ce601814169e6e59 | 6.7 s | Then the pilot brought the four gifts to Delos: gold, black glass, white marble and the vine-crown of Ariadne. |
+| ariadne | de9705478f42d399 | 8.9 s | Gold, obsidian, marble and the vine. The pillars are raised. Delos stands where Leto found her rest, and the god's light burns in the Circle. |
+| ariadne | 148765fe63dca5cf | 10.4 s | One rite remains. On Keros, the old people broke their marble figures and laid them down, all together, in one place. We still do. Bring the offering there. |
+| kilon | da97dc6613bc94fa | 8.2 s | Keros: a small island where nobody lives, and where, for a thousand years, the people of the Isles came to break what they had made. |
+| kilon | a0a080306af85a5f | 11.8 s | They broke the white figures with their folded arms and their quiet faces, and laid the pieces down together, as their fathers had for a thousand years. No one now knows why. Perhaps it does not matter. |
+| ariadne | 72d7d8263d5b8963 | 6.4 s | The Isles are one circle again. Take our thanks, guest - and our gold, which is honest. |
 | kilon | 36d0dc68e9a5c678 | 1.5 s | The thread is in your hands. |
hunks.title: The empire stories
